question: How does my phone think?
teaser: Follow a phone down to the switch that does all the work, and then to the crystal that the switch is cut from.

stops.title: A phone, opened up
text: A phone is a slab about 7 to 8 millimetres thick with a screen, a battery, a camera, radios and one main circuit board. The part that does the "thinking" is a single chip on that board.
It does not think the way you do. It follows instructions, one tiny step after another, very fast.
stops.notice: The view shows the phone taken apart. Click the parts to name them, and look for the main circuit board that holds the chips.

stops.title: The main chip
text: This is the system-on-chip, a die of silicon with an area of roughly 100 square millimetres. Processor cores, graphics, an engine for AI, an image processor and memory controllers all share it.
A chip like this holds roughly ten to twenty billion transistors.
stops.model: A schematic floor plan: the blocks are in plausible places, but this is not the layout of any one real chip.
stops.notice: Click a block, such as the CPU cluster or the GPU, to see what it is for.

stops.title: One processor core
text: A core runs a program one instruction at a time. For each one it fetches the instruction, works out what it means, and then carries it out.
Many instructions are in progress at once, like cars on an assembly line, which is called pipelining.
stops.model: Schematic: the blocks show the job each part does, not the real arrangement.
stops.notice: Find the block called the arithmetic logic unit. That is where the adding and comparing happens.

deeper.label: How a CPU runs one instruction

stops.title: Logic gates
text: Down here the arithmetic is built from tiny circuits called logic gates. A NAND gate gives the answer 0 only when both of its inputs are 1, and every other logic function can be built from NAND gates.
Chain enough of them together and you can add numbers, compare them and move them around.
stops.notice: Click an adder or a gate. Each one is a few switches wired together.

stops.title: The simplest circuit
text: The inverter turns a 1 into a 0 and a 0 into a 1. It is made of two switches, one that pulls the output up and one that pulls it down, and only one is on at a time.
Because of that, hardly any current flows except at the moment of switching, which is why chips can have billions of them.
stops.notice: Find the two transistors. When the input is high, one conducts and pulls the output low.

stops.title: A transistor shaped like a fin
text: Each switch is a transistor. In a modern chip the current flows through a thin vertical fin of silicon, and the gate wraps around three sides of the fin to control it better.
A voltage on the gate attracts electrons into the fin and turns the switch on. Remove the voltage and it turns off.
stops.model: A simplified drawing of a FinFET, not a measured layout.
stops.notice: Find the fin, the gate wrapped around it, and the source and drain at its two ends.

stops.title: The silicon crystal
text: The part of the transistor where current flows is a sliver of near-perfect crystal. It is silicon, whose atoms sit in a regular pattern, and the electrons that carry the current move through it.
So the answer to the question is that your phone does not think with anything exotic. It shifts electrons through billions of switches, and logic does the rest.
stops.notice: Look at the regular pattern of atoms. A crystal like this is what the whole chip is cut from.

answer: A phone does not think: it follows instructions, and every step is made of billions of tiny silicon switches that electrons turn on and off.
unknown: Nothing about how the chip works is mysterious. What is open is how much smaller and faster such switches can be made before atoms and heat set the limit.
